newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Greenspan remarks market focus.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Greenspan remarks market focus.

text.p: The prices of U.S. government securities could face downward pressure next week as the market pensively looks to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's congressional testimony.

Greenspan begins his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony Wednesday morning and players will have little in the way of data to distract them prior to that time. The market also will have to absorb a new round of supply in addition to its regular three- and six-month bill auction Monday with two- and five-year note sales on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.

Market participants will scrutinize the central bank chief's comments to try to discern if his views on the economy have changed. In particular, his views on wage inflation and stock market valuations levels will be watched.

Steven Wieting, economist at Smith Barney Inc., said market participants expected Greenspan to sound hawkish, one of many negative factors for the market in the near term. However, he said the obstacles were surmountable and his firm remains optimistic longer term.
"We don't think he (Greenspan) will suddenly change his tone on being cautious on inflation," Wieting said.
Challenges ahead include February economic data that a lot of observers expected would be quite strong.

"Our preliminary estimate is for a 350,000 nonfarm payroll increase for February. There was a lot of weakness in the January report with hours worked and some of that activity may be pushed into February," Wieting said.

But long term Wieting said there wasn't likely to be any major acceleration in prices, a stronger U.S. dollar had helped lower import prices (excluding petroleum products) almost 2.0 percent from last year and oil prices were well off their highs.

"Labor costs just aren't being passed through and there are a number of reasons we don't think this situation is going to turn around. There's likely to be progress on a balanced budget later this year and bond yields should continue lower," Wieting said.

Aside from Greenspan, there was little slated for release. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index was set for Wednesday and durable goods orders were due early Thursday. Initial claims, also on Thursday, will be closely watched for signs of more weakness. The four-week moving average has been declining, indicative of tightening labor markets.

"I don't expect him (Greenspan) to say anything shocking. The smell of December's 'irrational exuberance' comment still lingers in the air," said Brian Westbury, chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc. "The bottom line is the economy continues to grow as the expansion moves into its seventh year -- the second long expansion in a row."

Westbury said the central bank chief would probably credit stable monetary policy as a key to this and stress the need for vigilance in fighting inflation. With low inflation, moderate growth and a vigilant Fed, the bond market should be in very good shape after the testimony concludes, he said.
Westbury hoped Greenspan would touch upon monetary base growth rates, which have surged recently. He expected Greenspan to say the economy was pushing against some capacity constraints, but not all.

"The bond market should be more worried about inflation if it had a Fed that wasn't worried," Westbury said. He saw the Fed getting through 1997 without tightening, and perhaps even easing, monetary policy.
Thursday will also see existing home sales and the revised real fourth quarter gross domestic product.
